warmup.text: In Chapter 17, Isaac goes back to visit his family. The poem today repeats one line, and a new picture follows it each time. Watch what the second picture adds. Then think about something that keeps coming back in Isaac's story.

words.text: Today you decide which root each word carries: see, or look. Then sort the sound alike words by the job they do. Does the word show who owns something, name a thing, or squeeze two words together? Then five new words in the spyglass.

reading.text: Read Chapter 17 in your book. Watch how Isaac spends the day with his family, and what he says when it is time to go. Then read the Read Like a Writer sentence about Nani Humma, and finish with the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapter 17, then your first revision. Take the first moment from your plan. Add one detail you can see, hear, smell or feel, and one comparison. Show the old version first, then the new one.

hook.q: When someone you love leaves for a long time, what do you say?

options.reply: That is what most of us say. Isaac's family says something different. Here is why:
That is close to what Isaac's family says. Here is how Isaac explains it:
Sometimes a hug says it all. Isaac's family has words for it too. Here is what Isaac says:

reveal.line: Choctaws never say “good-bye.” There is no word for it.
reveal.then: As you read Chapter 17, find what Choctaws say instead, and what it means.

do: Read today's skill.
Tap the lens you will use today.
Watch for things from earlier chapters that come back in this one.
how.why: A theme is built from things that return, not from one moment.
how.use: You will use this for question 3.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Find the pronoun that could mean two people in the second.
Fix it out loud, then tap Check My Work.
how.why: A pronoun like he or they should point to only one person or group.

do: Read the poem out loud once.
Find the line or picture that comes back.
Read Think About It and keep your answer in mind.
how.why: When a poet repeats something, each new picture adds to the idea. That is how a theme grows.

do: Ask: does this word have see or look in it?
Tap a word, then tap its root and meaning.
Match all four.
how.why: vis and vid lean toward what is seen. spect leans toward looking.

do: Read each sentence from the book.
Look for clues around the word.
Tap a word, then tap its meaning.
how.why: Clues in a sentence can tell you what a word means.

do: Count the halves that could stand alone.
Tap the complex sentence in each pair.
Label the three sentences in the box and explain.
how.why: Two halves that can stand alone make a compound sentence. One makes it complex.

do: Read each word.
Ask: owner, thing, or two words squeezed?
Tap a word, then tap its column.
how.why: Meaning picks the spelling, not sound.

do: Read Chapter 17 first.
Answer each question in 2 or more sentences.
Use details from the chapter as evidence.
how.why: These questions check what happened and what it shows about the people in the story.

do: Copy the first moment from your plan.
Add one detail you can see, hear, smell or feel.
Add one comparison with like or as.
how.why: One strong detail can put a reader inside the moment.
how.use: Next lesson you will revise the second moment.

do: Read what courage means.
Read the example from this week.
After you read, fill in your courage log at the end of this tab.
Read the chapter introduction below.
Open your book and read Chapter 17.
Then do the Virtue Watch and the Read Like a Writer box below.

glossary.meaning: a picture a writer puts in your mind with words
a big idea a book shows about people, said as a full sentence

miss.effect: An effect is a result. It names a thing (a noun).
miss.it's: It's is two words squeezed: it is. Try saying it is in the sentence.
miss.its: Its shows ownership, with no apostrophe: the wagon and its wheels.
miss.principle: A principle is a rule or belief. It names a thing.
miss.there: There points to a place: over there.
miss.they're: They're is two words squeezed: they are.

game.title: The Spyglass
game.sub: This week's word game · 5 words today
game.look: Isaac sees what other people cannot see. In this game, a brass spyglass looks at one word at a time. First tap the root hiding inside it: vis or vid means see, and spect means look. The root lights up. Then tap what the word means. Every word you get adds a star to the spyglass.

do: Look at the word in the spyglass.
Tap the root you find inside it.
Tap what the word means.
Tap Next word.
how.why: If you can spot a root, you can work out a long word you have never seen.

opts: to look at again and make better
words.why: Yes. To revise is to see your work again and improve it.
Yes. Spectacles is an old word for glasses.
Yes. Something evident is easy to see. vid = see.
Yes. A prospect is something ahead that you look toward.

opts: to watch over other people's work
words.why: Yes. To supervise is to watch over others as they work.

art.title: Twilight in the Wilderness
art.alt: A painting of a fiery red and orange sunset sky over dark hills, a river and trees.
art.look: Frederic Edwin Church painted this sunset in 1860 from his sketches of the northern woods. It is far from Isaac's road, but it matches the end of Chapter 17: “Soon the sky streaked red and the sun dipped below the hills.”
art.lookBtn: Tap to learn about this painting
art.creator: Frederic Edwin Church

cards.title: Choctaw words in Chapters 16 and 17
cards.intro: Isaac tells his story in English, but some Choctaw words stay in it.

items.meaning: Thank you. Isaac says it to Nani Humma in Chapter 16.
Choctaw corn soup. Isaac's family eats it together at noon.
items.line: It was the best bowl of corn soup I'd ever had.

items.meaning: What Choctaws say instead of good-bye: I will see you again, in the future.

cards.note: The narrator does not say these words aloud. Choctaw has its own sounds, and we would rather not teach them wrong.

Joseph sneaks into camp before sunrise to take Isaac to see his family.
Luke gives Joseph his blowgun and tells him to take care of Isaac.
